summary: For 5–6 year olds (roughly UK Y1, US K–Grade 1), introduce multiplication as repeated addition of EQUAL groups ('a groups of b'): 3 groups of 4 = 4+4+4. Build on the skip counting children are learning at this age (counting in 2s, 5s and 10s, e.g. 2, 4, 6 = one, two, three twos); when using groups of 4, introduce counting in fours alongside the groups (4, 8, 12 = one, two, three fours) rather than assuming it is already known. Keep the group structure visible from real objects → pictures/arrays → the repeated-addition sentence → later the × symbol. Stress that the groups must be equal (the defining feature children most often drop) and keep the two numbers distinct (how many groups vs how many in each). Repeated addition is the correct entry model at this age, but it is a model, not the whole meaning of multiplication.
misconceptions: Adding groups that are not equal and still calling it multiplication — losing the 'equal groups' defining property.
Reading 3 × 4 as 3 + 4 (confusing multiplication with a single addition).
Counting the number of groups when asked for the total, or vice versa — muddling the two roles.

Believing multiplication is ONLY repeated addition (a seed of later trouble with fractions/decimals/scaling) — at this age fine, but teachers should model equal-groups language, not 'times means add lots'.
Miscounting the total by losing track of which groups have been counted (no systematic skip count).

activities.title: Equal-groups builder: watch groups, sentence and number line move together
steps: Add groups one at a time. With each group added, watch three things update together: a new '+4' joins a running repeated-addition sentence (4, then 4+4, then 4+4+4), a jump advances along a number line (4→8→12), and a total counter climbs.

Notice where each number-line jump lands (4, 8, 12) and say these numbers as counting in fours; also try a group size of 2, 5 or 10 and compare where the jumps land with the skip counting you already know.
Use a collapse control to fold '4+4+4' into '3 groups of 4', then expand it back.
Try adding an unequal group (e.g. a group of 3 among the fours) and see it flagged as 'not equal groups yet'; fix it so all groups match.
activities.insight: '3 groups of 4', '4+4+4', and 'counting in fours three times' are three views of one and the same thing, and the groups must be equal for it to be multiplication.

activities.title: Make the groups yourself with real objects
steps: Physically make, for example, 3 groups of 2 counters.
Write the matching repeated-addition sentence 2+2+2 and point to where each '2' is in your groups.
Rebuild with a different number of groups (e.g. 4 groups of 2) and write the new sentence.
activities.insight: Each addend in the repeated-addition sentence corresponds to one equal group of objects.

activities.title: Number line and grouped objects side by side
steps: Place grouped objects (e.g. three groups of 4) next to a number line.
Draw equal jumps of 4 on the number line, landing on 4, 8, 12.
Say the totals as you jump and match each jump to a group.
activities.insight: Skip counting on a number line and repeated addition of equal groups are the same idea shown two ways.

activities.title: Match, sequence and fill in — a companion check
steps: Match an equal-groups picture to its repeated-addition sentence (e.g. three groups of 4 ↔ 4+4+4).
Spot and reject a picture of unequal groups offered as if it were '3 groups of 4'.
activities.insight: A matching/sequencing/fill-in task shows whether the picture–sentence–total link holds and whether unequal groups are correctly rejected; recognition here does not by itself build or vary the concept.

activities.title: Talk it through: 'how many wheels on 3 cars?'
steps: Answer an equal-groups question such as 'how many wheels on 3 cars with 4 wheels each?' by counting groups aloud.
Correct a partner who 'forgets' to keep the groups equal (e.g. gives one car 3 wheels).
Say the matching sentence, e.g. 4+4+4, and give the total.
activities.insight: Equal-groups language ('3 groups of 4') describes real situations and must keep every group the same size.

checkQuestion: Here are 3 plates with 2 cakes on each. How many cakes altogether? After the child answers, ask: can you show me why that's the same as 2 + 2 + 2?
checkAnswer: 6 cakes. A child reasoning correctly sees the three plates as three EQUAL groups of 2 and connects '3 groups of 2' to the repeated addition 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 — explaining that each plate contributes one 2 to the sum.
